title: Panic Attacks: What They Are and How to Stop Them
description: What's happening in your body during a panic attack, how to stop one in progress, and treatment options to prevent them from happening.

content.text: Your heart is racing. You can't breathe. You might be dying. You're not—you're having a panic attack. Here's what's happening and how to regain control.
What a Panic Attack Actually Is
A panic attack is your fight-or-flight response misfiring. Your brain perceives danger when there is none and floods your body with adrenaline. The symptoms are terrifying but not dangerous.

items: Fear of dying or losing control

content.text: Symptoms typically peak within 10 minutes and resolve within 20-30 minutes.
How to Stop a Panic Attack
Remind yourself: 'This is a panic attack. It's uncomfortable but not dangerous. It will pass.'
Paradoxically, accepting the panic rather than resisting it helps it pass faster. Fighting it adds more adrenaline.
If possible, don't flee the situation. Escaping teaches your brain the situation was dangerous, making future panic more likely.
It's common to mistake a panic attack for a heart attack. Key differences:

items: Panic: sharp/stabbing chest pain | Heart attack: pressure/squeezing
Panic: symptoms peak then fade | Heart attack: symptoms persist or worsen
Panic: triggered by stress/anxiety | Heart attack: often with exertion
Panic: tingling in extremities | Heart attack: pain radiating to arm/jaw

content.text: If you're unsure, or if this is your first episode of chest pain, seek emergency care. Better safe than sorry.
CBT for panic disorder is highly effective. You'll learn to identify triggers, challenge catastrophic thoughts, and gradually face avoided situations.

Panic attacks are terrifying but not dangerous. They're your body's alarm system going haywire. With proper treatment—usually CBT, sometimes medication—most people can eliminate or significantly reduce panic attacks.
